html:
The Hujum, meaning "assault", was a Soviet Communist Party campaign launched in 1927 to unveil the women of Central Asia and end their seclusion. It was strongest in Uzbekistan.

Many urban women there wore the paranja, a long robe over the head, with a heavy horsehair veil over the face. The Party saw veiling, seclusion and child marriage as signs of backwardness. On International Women's Day, 8 March 1927, it organised mass meetings where thousands of women threw their veils into bonfires.

The backlash was fierce. Many people saw the campaign as an attack on Islam and on family honour. Unveiled women were insulted, beaten, and in many cases murdered, sometimes by their own relatives, and some women put the veil back on. The Party then eased off. Under Soviet rule the veil faded only slowly, over the next decades, through schooling and women's work outside the home.
sum: The Hujum, meaning "assault", was a Soviet Communist Party campaign launched in 1927 to unveil the women of Central Asia and end their seclusion. It was strongest in Uzbekistan.
